newsitem.title: CHINA: Pressure mounts on HK govt in courtroom battle.
newsitem.headline: Pressure mounts on HK govt in courtroom battle.

text.p: Hong Kong's political fate hung by a thread on Thursday as a court case adjourned pending a judgment next week that could plunge the post-colonial government into a constitutional crisis.
The landmark court challenge centres on the China-appointed Provisional Legislative Council, which top lawyers have argued violates Hong Kong's new constitution.
Wrapping up the appeal court hearing, a top government lawyer warned that any bid by the court to declare the interim chamber illegal would invite chaos and jeopardise the entire legal system.
Presiding Chief Judge Justice Patrick Chan said his panel would make a judgment next Tuesday.
Legal experts said it was up to Chan's team whether to rule on the legality of the legislature, a case that grew from a criminal conspiracy trial into a constitutional conundrum.

Lawyers argued that three defendants charged with criminal conspiracy should be set free because the pre-handover laws under which they were charged ceased to be valid on July 1 when the chamber failed formally to adopt them, leaving a legal vacuum.
The argument throws into doubt the status and legality of the Provisional Legislature, installed to replace an elected chamber when Britain handed its 156-year-old colony back to China on July 1.
The challenge is at the heart of the legal system and Hong Kong institutions, as the chamber has endorsed the appointment of senior judges and passed crucial laws since it was sworn in 24 days ago.
The court hearing entered its third day on Thursday with former Bar chairwoman Gladys Li leading top lawyers in the attack on Solicitor-General Daniel Fung.

In a packed court room, Fung argued that the provisional chamber, cobbled together by a China-appointed body and endorsed by China's parliament in April, was a legal necessity with the end of British rule and the entry of the new sovereign power, China.

Fung said China axed original plans to allow the 1995 chamber to serve its full four-year term beyond the handover because 1995 electoral rules spearheaded by the last colonial governor Chris Patten did not conform to Sino-British agreements.
"The through-train was envisioned, but not unconditional," Fung said.
He said it was not up to Hong Kong courts to rule on decisions of China's parliament, and any attempt to declare the chamber null and void would lead to havoc.
"If your lordships were to rule against us...there would be no legal system. The rule of law exists to protect people, and cannot be used to destroy society," he said.

Li said judges had the right to rule on the legality of the chamber, which she argued had no basis in Hong Kong's new constitution and violated 1990 legal rules for the first post-handover assembly set by China's parliament.
Legal experts said Tuesday's judgment might be confined to the status of the criminal case from which it sprang.
Fresh challenges could arise if the court fails to produce a binding judgment on the Provisional Legislature.
Meanwhile, a local poll showed that more Hong Kong people think political conditions and the rule of law have been deteriorating since China took over on July 1.
Some 21 percent of the people polled said the rule of law had weakened, while only 5.8 percent thought it was stronger. Some percent 44 percent were less confident in the rule of law.
Chief Executive Tung Chee-hwa has expressed confidence that his government will win the court case, but he said it would abide by the ruling either way.
He is also grappling with a host of problems ranging from illegal immigrant children from China to anger over his rolling back of civil freedoms and labour rights laws.
